articles.fullText:
Rooted in sovereign equality, demand-driven development and mutual benefit, the China-Africa partnership stands as an ever-evolving and exemplary blueprint for advancing the empowerment of the Global South. This framework delivers tangible socioeconomic results while redefining how emerging economies organize collective agency within a landscape marked by fracturing global supply chains, inequitable multilateral financial rules and widening development divides.
China has been Africa's largest trading partner for 17 consecutive years, and the bilateral trade volume exceeded $348 billion in 2025, marking an annual increase of 17.7 percent. The cooperation framework increasingly prioritizes African industrialization, moving beyond simple commodity trade to support local manufacturing, value chain development and job creation.
Established in 2000, the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation has delivered successive action plans that have launched thousands of livelihood-focused "small yet beautiful" projects spanning agriculture, healthcare, digital connectivity and vocational training. By 2024, more than 220,000 African professionals had received technical training through Chinese programs, while agricultural technology demonstration centers have boosted food security for millions of rural households across sub-Saharan Africa. Cooperation with China comes without the political conditions that are often associated with Western financial mechanisms.
Africa faces growing debt vulnerabilities and an alternative development finance architecture is urgently required. That's why the New Development Bank under the BRICS framework presents a viable alternative financing channel. Since its founding, the NDB has approved over $40 billion in project financing across member and partner states, including multiple sustainable infrastructure initiatives in Egypt, Bangladesh and South Africa. Deepening coordination between FOCAC mechanisms and BRICS financial institutions creates new avenues to scale affordable, long-term capital for African economies and extend comparable opportunities to other Global South regions.
At the 18th BRICS Summit held in New Delhi on Sept 12-13, leaders adopted a joint declaration reaffirming their commitment to inclusive global governance and multilateralism, while pledging enhanced cultural and people-to-people exchanges.
The summit underscored an agenda centered on improving global governance and fostering sustainable, inclusive global economic growth, while calling for international and regional peace and security. It has amplified the collective voice of the Global South and carries far-reaching implications for Africa.
BRICS has expanded significantly in recent years, with Egypt and Ethiopia among the African countries that have joined the group, embedding African perspectives firmly within the group's decision-making processes. The summit's priorities — improving global governance, revitalizing global trade, deepening economic cooperation and strengthening regional security — align closely with core African demands for fairer global trading rules, predictable investment flows and African-led conflict resolution frameworks.
The New Delhi summit also provided a timely diplomatic window to draw broader lessons from China-Africa engagement and explore how they could inform broader BRICS+strategy for the collective advancement of the Global South, offering a platform to translate the shared aspirations of developing nations into coordinated, actionable outcomes. And as China is set to take over the BRICS presidency in 2027, the China-Africa partnership will serve as an institutional anchor for the next phase of Greater BRICS cooperation.
Looking beyond the summit, a key priority should be advancing coordinated South-South value chain integration. For decades, most Global South economies have remained trapped at the lower end of global production networks, exporting raw materials while importing finished manufactured goods. China-Africa industrial parks and special economic zone partnerships offer a template to break this cycle, supporting local processing capacity to boost export competitiveness. BRICS nations can jointly promote such industrial cooperation models across Africa, Latin America and Southeast Asia, facilitating technology transfer and shared manufacturing capacity among developing economies. Parallel progress on local currency settlement mechanisms, being explored and implemented in various forms among BRICS members and their partners, can reduce systemic exposure to currency volatility and unilateral financial sanctions.
On regional security, the China-Africa framework prioritizes African solutions to African problems, rejecting external military interventionism and prioritizing political mediation of conflicts. This principle aligns with core BRICS consensus on advancing inclusive security governance. At the New Delhi summit, BRICS leaders reaffirmed the importance of advocating greater African representation within the United Nations Security Council and other multilateral bodies, a longstanding demand shared widely across the Global South. Unified advocacy for reform of global governance institutions remains essential to dismantle outdated power structures that systematically marginalize developing countries.
As the influence of BRICS expands, narratives questioning the intentions of South-South partnerships continue to circulate. Yet the lived experience across African nations demonstrates that the China-Africa model operates on fundamentally different terms from traditional donor-recipient hierarchies. Cooperation projects are negotiated bilaterally, aligned with national development strategies set by African governments, and designed to support long-term self-reliance rather than permanent dependency. This partnership advocates a multipolar international order where every nation, large or small, enjoys equal decision-making rights.
Moving forward, amplifying Global South voices demands sustained, institutionalized dialogue rather than ad-hoc diplomatic coordination. BRICS can draw on FOCAC's regular ministerial conferences, thematic working groups and people-to-people exchange frameworks to build permanent consultation channels with Global South communities. Expanded collaboration in climate finance, digital transformation and food security — all critical areas for Africa and developing regions — can demonstrate how collective South-South action delivers tangible progress toward the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
The China-Africa partnership, developed over two decades of effective collaboration, serves as a practical model for Global South nations to unite and advance shared interests. Its foundation of equality, mutual respect and win-win development presents a viable alternative to hierarchical international relations. Applying the lessons from this partnership to the commitments made at the September summit — and carrying them forward under China's 2027 BRICS presidency — could not only strengthen Africa-BRICS ties but also initiate a new era of unified Global South action, reshaping international trade, finance and security for the future.

articles.fullText:
Veterinarians from the Turkish Diyanet Foundation (TDV) examine livestock to assess health compliance in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, May 26, 2026. /CFP
Improved weather forecasts could help livestock farmers prepare for increasingly severe droughts, but new research suggests they will have limited impact unless vulnerable households also have the means to act on the warnings.
An international team led by the University of Sydney and Imperial College London says combining climate information with measures such as livestock feed, drought insurance, targeted financial assistance and better market access could help protect some of southern Africa's poorest pastoral communities from climate shocks.
The study, published in Nature Sustainability, comes as the region prepares for the potential impacts of a powerful El Nino weather event.
Researchers warn that increasing climate variability could deepen existing inequalities across southern Africa's rangelands, where millions of people depend on cattle, sheep and goats for income, food and household savings.
Forecasts are not enough
Lead researcher Dr. Matt Clark said the challenge was not simply a lack of access to climate information, but the limited ability of poorer farmers to respond to it.
"If the forecasts prove correct and we see a near-record El Nino develop, we expect this will amplify inequalities across southern African rangelands," Clark said.
While wealthier livestock owners can sell animals before drought conditions worsen and later rebuild their herds, poorer pastoralists often lack the financial resources to reduce their herds or purchase supplementary feed.
This can leave them with little choice but to keep livestock on increasingly degraded grazing land, increasing the risk of livestock deaths and further loss of household wealth.
The consequences can extend beyond individual families, affecting food security, livelihoods and the health of fragile rangelands.
The researchers say practical support can enable farmers to act on forecasts before drought takes hold, potentially reducing both economic losses and environmental damage.
Combining adaptation measures
The team used detailed modeling to examine how pastoral households across Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe might respond to increasing rainfall variability.
The researchers combined projected rainfall data from European climate models with information on livestock, vegetation and household wealth.
Their first simulation examined a business-as-usual scenario and found that greater rainfall variability could reduce household wealth, increase livestock losses, degrade grasslands and widen inequality.
A second simulation tested different adaptation measures. Climate forecasts on their own produced only modest benefits because many poorer households could not afford to act on the information. Risk-smoothing measures alone could also create environmental trade-offs.
But when climate information was combined with practical and financial support, the researchers found that households were better able to prepare for drought while reducing pressure on rangelands.
A worker stands next to Ndama cattle at the Nyanga Ranch in Tchibanga, Gabon, September 13, 2025. /CFP
The model also suggested that adaptation could spread between neighboring communities as farmers learned from one another and adopted successful strategies.
Dr. Gina Arena of Conservation International's Herding for Health initiative said greater climate uncertainty was increasing the risks faced by pastoral communities.
"It's that with greater uncertainty in climate comes greater risk," she said, adding that research could help identify effective decisions while reducing the risks associated with implementing them.
The researchers say the approach does not necessarily require new technology. Instead, existing forecasting systems need to be linked to programs that give vulnerable communities the resources to respond.
Clark said the framework could also be applied beyond southern Africa, including in Australia and other regions where livestock producers face increasingly unpredictable rainfall.
The findings highlight a broader challenge for climate adaptation: early warnings can save lives and livelihoods only when the people receiving them have the resources to act.

As countries seek to expand cleaner energy while maintaining reliable and affordable power supplies, energy security, access and technological innovation are increasingly linked.
Solar panels and wind turbines on the grassland in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, north China. 
At the 11th BRICS Energy Ministers' Meeting in Gurugram, India, energy ministers identified three broad areas for cooperation: energy security and sustainability, energy access and equity, and technology and innovation.
BRICS brings together 11 emerging and developing economies, with cooperation spanning areas including energy, science and technology, trade and finance. Its members have different energy resources, development priorities and energy systems, shaping the way they approach these common challenges.
A high-rise office building topped with solar panels at an industrial park in Zhengzhou, Henan Province, central China, August 18, 2026. 
Balancing security, access and transition
The energy agenda reflects the different circumstances of BRICS members. The ministers reaffirmed the importance of respecting national circumstances, development priorities and energy pathways, while calling for diversified and resilient energy systems and supply chains.
The meeting also highlighted universal access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy. Affordable financing and capacity building were identified as part of efforts to support emerging markets and developing economies. At the same time, members discussed cooperation in renewable energy, biofuels, hydrogen, energy storage, carbon capture, energy efficiency and other technologies.
Rather than setting out a single model for the energy transition, the agenda emphasizes cooperation across different technologies and national energy systems.
Construction site of the Gansu Huitong 300MW/1,200MWh standalone energy storage power station in Shandan County, Gansu Province, northwest China, August 25, 2026. 
Smart grids and energy storage
Smart grids and energy storage offer a more specific example of that approach.
A smart grid uses digital technologies, sensors, automation and data analysis to monitor and manage electricity systems. Energy storage facilities can hold electricity for later use, helping power systems manage changes in supply and demand. Both can become increasingly relevant as renewable energy is integrated into electricity systems.
During India's 2026 BRICS chairship, members launched the BRICS Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage under the BRICS Energy Research Cooperation Platform. The center is designed as a voluntary collaborative platform for knowledge sharing, capacity building, exchanges on policy and regulatory practices, and pilot initiatives.
Members also adopted the BRICS Guiding Principles on Smart Grids and Energy Storage, recognizing the role of modern, resilient and digitally enabled power systems in supporting reliable and affordable energy access and integrating renewable energy and emerging technologies.
For BRICS countries, the initiative provides a channel to compare experience and build technical capacity around common challenges. Its practical impact will depend on how knowledge exchanges and proposed pilot initiatives develop across different national power systems.

China will maintain a relatively ample workforce and will press ahead with efforts to build a fertility-friendly society, Lei Haichao, minister of the National Health Commission, said on Monday.
China's total population has declined for four consecutive years, but the nation remains home to 1.405 billion people and will continue to be a major demographic power for years to come, Lei said at a news conference in Beijing held by the State Council Information Office.
With more than 10 million students enrolling in colleges and universities each year amid a boom in the higher education sector, China is building an expanding and highly skilled workforce, Lei said.
Official data shows that, by the end of 2025, China had about 851.36 million people ages 16 to 59, and that group had an average of 11.3 years of schooling, up 0.1 year from a year earlier.
Lei added that the annual number of newborns has remained at about 8 million despite an overall downward trend.
"Compared with other developed and developing countries, very few have births at this level, so China will still have a relatively ample labor force in the future," he said.
Lei noted that China will continue to roll out fertility-friendly measures to ease the burden of childbirth, child-rearing and education.
Among the latest fertility support policies are the rollout of a fertility subsidy, which has so far benefited more than 30 million families, and the establishment of nearly 12,600 early pregnancy care clinics nationwide, providing counseling and assessments.
He said that the nation will work harder over the next five years to integrate nursery and kindergarten care services and support communities and employers in setting up more convenient and affordable nursery care facilities.
Under the national health plan released in July for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period, one goal is to raise the nursery care enrollment rate by 6 percentage points for children age 3 and under, Lei said.
It is also important to promote a positive view of marriage and fertility, he added.
Guo Yanhong, vice-minister of the National Health Commission, said that the authorities will continue to improve early pregnancy care, as well as the prevention and treatment of birth defects and developmental problems.
"We will also step up efforts to build fertility-friendly hospitals and improve conditions in obstetric, neonatal and pediatric wards. Each province will be supported in building at least one high-level maternal and child health institution to strengthen fertility support functions," she said.
Health authorities said that China has built the world's largest medical service system. As part of efforts to provide life-cycle healthcare services, priorities in the coming years include improving pediatric care and early childhood development services, and building more child-friendly hospitals.
Lei said that China aims this year to add 1,000 more community- and township-level healthcare centers offering pediatric care.
By the end of 2026, more than 95 percent of such grassroots health facilities are expected to provide pediatric diagnosis and treatment, he added.

By 2031, the share of New Development Bank (NDB) projects financed in local currencies "will exceed 45%," Russian Finance Minister and NDB Board of Governors Chair Anton Siluanov said in May. It now stands at 30%, he added at the bank's Annual Meeting.
It's a mission the bank was built for. Established in 2015 by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, the Shanghai-based NDB exists to mobilize resources for infrastructure and sustainable development across the Global South.
India's state-owned REC Limited is the latest case in point, securing an NDB loan to build renewable energy power plants, as the country expands clean energy and steps back from fossil fuels.
Wang Youming, a researcher at the China Institute of International Studies, said stronger use of local currencies in trade, investment and foreign-exchange reserves could reduce developing countries' reliance on the US dollar.
It can also shield economies from external shocks, strengthen fiscal and financial autonomy, and mitigate politically motivated sanctions, he added.
By June 2026, the NDB had approved 139 projects totaling about $42.9 billion. According to the lender, the projects have helped increase clean energy capacity by 2,400 megawatts, cut annual carbon dioxide emissions by 14.7 million tonnes, and supported the construction of 35,000 housing units, 43 schools, 1,400 kilometers of tunnels and canals, and 40,400 kilometers of roads.
In Brazil, the Pará State Water and Sanitation Infrastructure Development Project focuses on protecting drinking water, reducing pollution and restoring ecosystems. In India, the Delhi-Ghaziabad-Meerut Regional Rapid Transit System Project aims to improve public transport, ease congestion and promote low-carbon mobility.
Beyond green infrastructure, the NDB has been developing new financing tools to address long-standing challenges – limited access to capital and exposure to exchange-rate volatility.
The NDB is not the only BRICS mechanism strengthening financial resilience. The BRICS Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA), established in 2015 with an initial reserve pool of $100 billion, provides a financial safety net for members facing short-term balance-of-payments pressures.
China accounts for 41% of its resources. The CRA complements existing global safety nets by giving BRICS countries an extra mechanism to respond to crises.
The NDB is also expanding beyond physical infrastructure. In June, Uzbekistan became the NDB's 10th member. Roman Sherov, vice president of the NDB, said the bank would incorporate digitalization and AI into its investments, with a focus on AI-powered digital finance over the next five years.

俄罗斯财政部长、新开发银行理事会主席安东·西卢阿诺夫在5月表示，到2031年，新开发银行（NDB）以本币融资的项目占比“将超过45%”。他在该银行的年会上补充说，目前这一比例为30%。这正是这家银行为之而建的使命。新开发银行于2015年由巴西、俄罗斯、印度、中国和南非共同成立，总部位于上海，旨在为整个全球南方的基础设施和可持续发展调动资源。印度国有企业REC有限公司就是最新的例证，该公司获得了新开发银行的贷款，用于建设可再生能源发电厂，而印度正在扩大清洁能源并逐步摆脱化石燃料。

中国国际问题研究院研究员王友明表示，在贸易、投资和外汇储备中更多地使用本币，可以减少发展中国家对美元的依赖。他补充说，这还能使各经济体免受外部冲击，增强财政和金融自主权，并减轻出于政治动机的制裁影响。截至2026年6月，新开发银行已批准139个项目，总额约429亿美元。据该银行称，这些项目帮助增加了2400兆瓦的清洁能源装机容量，每年减少1470万吨二氧化碳排放，并支持建设了3.5万套住房、43所学校、1400公里的隧道和运河以及4.04万公里的道路。在巴西，帕拉州供水和卫生基础设施发展项目侧重于保护饮用水、减少污染和恢复生态系统。

在印度，德里-加济阿巴德-密拉特区域快速交通系统项目旨在改善公共交通、缓解拥堵并促进低碳出行。除了绿色基础设施之外，新开发银行一直在开发新的融资工具，以应对长期存在的挑战——资本获取渠道有限以及汇率波动风险。新开发银行并不是唯一增强金融韧性的金砖机制。金砖国家应急储备安排（CRA）于2015年设立，初始储备池为1000亿美元，为面临短期国际收支压力的成员国提供金融安全网。中国占其资源的41%。

金砖国家应急储备安排通过为金砖国家提供应对危机的额外机制，补充了现有的全球安全网。新开发银行也在向实体基础设施之外扩展。6月，乌兹别克斯坦成为新开发银行的第10个成员。新开发银行副行长罗曼·舍罗夫表示，该银行将把数字化和人工智能纳入其投资，并在未来五年重点关注人工智能驱动的数字金融。在本周末于新德里举行的第18届金砖国家峰会之前，圣保罗大学金砖研究小组协调员卢卡斯·恩里克斯·罗查在接受TV BRICS采访时表示，此次峰会可以成为围绕人工智能保障、绿色金融和数字支付基础设施交流想法、建立新伙伴关系的平台。
